title: Seed addition did not clearly strengthen the warming response of three plant traits in a ten-year tundra experiment
abstract: We tested whether seed supply increases the plant community response to warming. We used paired subplots in an independent ten-year Finnish tundra experiment with 56 plots, seed addition, warming, NPK addition and mammal exclusion. We measured warming-response amplification for community mean height, specific leaf area and leaf dry matter content. Seed addition changed all three traits. The squared warming-response length changed by -0.09 after seed addition (95% plot bootstrap limits -0.83 to 1.30). The interval permits a large increase. A randomization test found no clear warming effect on the paired seed response (p = 0.890), including a test across four treatment contexts (p = 0.658). Nutrient modification passed a three-test correction (adjusted p = 0.0063). An exploratory direct comparison put the squared nutrient interaction 3.47 units above the warming interaction (95% limits 0.33 to 8.18). Raw and log traits gave similar conclusions. The source paper already reported nutrient-dependent seed effects; our contribution is the multivariate release test, amplification estimate and direct comparison. The results support tests of local resource filters after arrival, but do not establish their share of the climate response gap. Limits include one site, one endpoint, seven plots per treatment cell, a pulse seed treatment, strong NPK addition, and functional traits rather than thermal affinity. Code, aggregate results, source hashes, retrieval instructions and a figure are included. Source records remain external.

display.caption: Paired seed effects and warming effects on three plant traits. Bars show ordinary 95% stratified plot bootstrap limits. Nutrients changed the seed effect more clearly than warming did at the tested treatment doses.
